steps.title: Friendly or polite you
steps.how_to: How to ask how someone is and get their attention, with tu for friends and Lei for strangers.
steps.intro: Italian has a friendly you and a polite you. You'll be able to pick the right one when you greet a shopkeeper, a neighbour or a stranger.
steps.notice: Come sta, Senta, scusi and E Lei are the polite set for strangers, shopkeepers and older people. Come stai, Senti, scusa and E tu are for friends. Tu with a shopkeeper sounds overfamiliar, so use Lei until they offer tu.

ask.it: Un signore anziano è vicino a te. Cosa dici?
ask.en: An older gentleman is next to you. What do you say?

mission.goal: Get a stranger's attention politely.

steps.title: Say how you are
steps.how_to: How to say you are well using sto, not sono.
steps.intro: Now you'll be able to answer when someone asks how you are. You'll say it in a shop, at a bar or in the piazza.
steps.notice: To say how you are, Italian uses sto. English 'I am fine' tempts you to say 'sono bene', which is wrong. Say 'sto bene'.

mission.goal: Tell the shopkeeper you are well and ask back.

steps.title: Hello at any hour
steps.how_to: How to greet people with buongiorno, buonasera or salve at the right time of day.
steps.intro: You'll be able to say hello at the right hour when you walk into a bar, a shop or a pharmacy. You'll also have one greeting for when you're unsure.
steps.notice: Buongiorno lasts until lunch or early afternoon, and buonasera covers the rest of the day. Buonanotte is only for bedtime, so say Buonasera when you walk into a bar at 9 p.m. Salve is safe when you don't know whether to use tu or Lei.
steps.context: Buonasera starts surprisingly early, around 3 or 4 p.m.

ask.it: Sono le dieci del mattino. Cosa dici entrando?
ask.en: It's ten in the morning. What do you say when you walk in?

ask.it: Sono le cinque del pomeriggio. Come saluti la signora?
ask.en: It's five in the afternoon. How do you greet the lady?

ask.it: Non sai se dare del tu o del Lei. Cosa dici?
ask.en: You don't know whether to use tu or Lei. What do you say?

mission.goal: Greet the barista when you walk in.

steps.title: Say goodbye nicely
steps.how_to: How to say goodbye and wish someone a good day or evening.
steps.intro: You'll be able to leave a shop or say goodbye to a neighbour with a warm wish. You'll also know how to answer when someone wishes you the same.

examples.it: Grazie, anche a te! Ci vediamo!

steps.notice: Buona giornata is for the day and buona serata is for the evening. To answer, say Altrettanto to anyone, or Anche a Lei or Anche a te depending on who you're talking to.
steps.context: Italians say goodbye when they leave a shop or a bar, and walking out in silence comes across as rude.

answer.it: Grazie, anche a te! Ci vediamo!

ask.it: È sera. Esci da un negozio. Cosa dici?
ask.en: It's evening. You're leaving a shop. What do you say?

mission.goal: Say goodbye to the shopkeeper as you leave.

steps.title: Saying you didn't understand
steps.how_to: How to say you didn't catch something, and that you got it.
steps.intro: You'll be able to tell someone you didn't understand and say when you finally do. You'll use it any time a conversation goes too fast, like at a shop counter.

examples.en: I only speak a little Italian.

steps.notice: To say no, put non right before the verb: non ho capito, with no word for "did". For something just said, use non ho capito, not non capisco.
steps.context: Most people are pleased that you're trying, so say it with a smile.

answer.en: I only speak a little Italian.

ask.it: Sono tre euro e venti. Ha capito?
ask.en: That's three euros twenty. Did you understand?

mission.goal: Tell the shopkeeper you didn't understand the price.

steps.title: Asking to repeat or slow down
steps.how_to: How to politely ask someone to repeat or speak more slowly.
steps.intro: You'll be able to ask someone to say it again, or slower. Use it at a counter when you've missed the price.

examples.en: Could you repeat that? (to a friend)

steps.notice: Può plus a basic verb makes a polite request, with no "to" in between: può ripetere. With a friend, change può to puoi.
steps.context: Many people speed up or switch to English, so a friendly "più piano, per favore" is normal and expected.

mission.goal: Ask the shopkeeper to repeat the price.

say.en: Sorry, could you repeat that, please?

steps.title: Asking about a word
steps.how_to: How to ask what a word means or how to say and spell it.
steps.intro: You'll be able to ask what an Italian word means, how to say something in Italian, and how to spell it. You'll use it when a word stops you at the bar or in a shop.

examples.en: How do you say “receipt” in Italian?

steps.notice: Cosa vuol dire? has no word for "does". Come si dice? and come si scrive? are fixed phrases, so just say them as they are.
steps.context: Italians say "Come?" or "Scusi?" for "Sorry?", because a bare "Cosa?" can sound blunt.

answer.it: Un po'. Come si dice “receipt” in italiano?
answer.en: A little. How do you say “receipt” in Italian?

mission.goal: Ask what a word means.

steps.title: Say your name
steps.how_to: How to give your name and ask for someone else's.
steps.intro: You'll be able to say your name and ask for theirs when you meet someone new. It works with your neighbour, in a bar, or on your first day of class.

examples.it: Piacere, Rosa. E Lei, come si chiama?
examples.en: Nice to meet you, I'm Rosa. And what's your name?

examples.it: Ciao, io sono Marco. E tu, come ti chiami?
examples.en: Hi, I'm Marco. And what's your name?
My name's Tom. Nice to meet you!
My name's Anna. Nice to meet you!

steps.notice: You give your name with mi chiamo and then just the name, nothing in between. The question starts with come, never cosa: Come ti chiami? or Come si chiama? for someone older.

ask.en: Nice to meet you, I'm Marco.

answer.en: Nice to meet you! My name's …
My name's … Nice to meet you!

mission.goal: Tell someone your name and ask theirs.

say.it: Mi chiamo … E Lei, come si chiama?
say.en: My name's … And what's your name?

steps.title: Say where you're from
steps.how_to: How to say your nationality and your city, and ask the same back.
steps.intro: You'll be able to say where you come from and ask someone else. It's one of the first questions people ask you here.

examples.it: No, sono americano, di Denver. E tu, di dove sei?
examples.en: No, I'm American, from Denver. And where are you from?

steps.notice: Just say sono, with no io in front. A woman says americana, and for the city you always use di, never da: Sono di Boston.
steps.context: 'Di dove sei?' is one of the first things Italians ask, because where you come from matters a lot here.

mission.goal: Say where you're from and ask the other person.

say.it: Sono americano, di … E tu, di dove sei?
say.en: I'm American, from … And where are you from?

steps.title: Say where you live
steps.how_to: How to say you live here and not on holiday.
steps.intro: You'll be able to say that you live here and give your street or city. It's what you say when someone takes you for a tourist.

examples.en: And are you here on holiday?

steps.notice: Abito ends in -o because it's you. Someone older asks Dove abita?, with -a, while a friend asks Dove abiti? For a city you say a: Abito a Firenze, not in Firenze.
steps.context: Saying you live here, not that you're on holiday, changes the conversation: people start treating you as a neighbour.

mission.goal: Tell someone you live here, not on holiday.

steps.title: Say how long you've been here
steps.how_to: How to say how long you've been in Italy.
steps.intro: You'll be able to say how long you've been here, and understand the welcome people give you. It's what you say right after telling someone you live here.

examples.it: Sono in Italia da tre settimane.
examples.en: I've been in Italy for three weeks.
I've been studying Italian for a month.

steps.notice: Italian uses the plain present with da for something that's still going on: Sono qui da tre settimane. Sono stato qui per tre settimane would mean the stay is over. People say ben arrivato to a man and ben arrivata to a woman.

ask.it: Sei in Italia da tre settimane?
ask.en: Have you been in Italy for three weeks?

answer.it: Sì, sono in Italia da tre settimane.
answer.en: Yes, I've been in Italy for three weeks.

answer.it: No, sono qui da tre settimane.
answer.en: No, I've been here for three weeks.

ask.en: Have you been studying Italian for a month?

answer.it: Sì, studio l'italiano da un mese.
answer.en: Yes, I've been studying Italian for a month.

mission.goal: Tell someone how long you've been in Italy.

say.en: I've been in Italy for … weeks.

steps.title: Say why you're here
steps.how_to: How to say why you're in Italy and what you do.
steps.intro: You'll be able to say that you're here to learn Italian, and whether you're retired or working. People ask this when they get to know you.
steps.notice: Sono qui per, plus a verb like imparare, tells why you're here. To say what you do, use Sono in pensione or Lavoro come and your job.

ask.en: Are you here to learn Italian?

answer.it: Sì, sono qui per imparare l'italiano.
answer.en: Yes, I'm here to learn Italian.

mission.goal: Tell someone why you're in Italy.

steps.title: A coffee, a croissant
steps.how_to: How to say "a" or "an" with food and drinks.
steps.intro: You'll be able to name what you want at the bar, with the right word for "a". You'll use it every time you order at the counter.

examples.it: Un cappuccino e un cornetto, per favore.
examples.en: A cappuccino and a croissant, please.

steps.notice: "A" changes with the word: un for most masculine words, uno before s plus a consonant, una for feminine ones. Un with an apostrophe, like un'aranciata, is only for feminine words, so say "uno spritz", not "un spritz".
steps.context: Cappuccino is a morning drink; after lunch Italians order an espresso.

mission.goal: Order a coffee at the counter.

steps.title: Two coffees, two croissants
steps.how_to: How to order more than one thing.
steps.intro: You'll be able to order for two or more people at the bar. It's what you say when you're out with a friend.

examples.it: Due cappuccini e due cornetti, per favore.
examples.en: Two cappuccinos and two croissants, please.

examples.it: Due tè e due spritz, per favore.
examples.en: Two teas and two spritzes, please.

steps.notice: Most words change their last vowel: cappuccino becomes cappuccini, cornetto becomes cornetti, spremuta becomes spremute. Words ending in an accented letter, like caffè and tè, or in a consonant, like spritz, stay the same. Never add an English s: say "due caffè", not "due caffès".

answer.it: Due cappuccini e due spremute, per favore.
answer.en: Two cappuccinos and two fresh juices, please.

mission.goal: Order two cappuccinos for you and a friend.

steps.title: I'd like, politely
steps.how_to: How to ask for something politely with vorrei.
steps.intro: You'll be able to ask politely for a drink, a glass of water or anything at the bar. You'll also hear the questions the barista asks back.

examples.en: I'd like a fresh orange juice.

examples.it: Vorrei un bicchiere d'acqua, per favore.
examples.en: I'd like a glass of water, please.
At the counter or at a table?

steps.notice: Vorrei means "I'd like" and works for anything you ask for. Don't say "voglio", "I want": it sounds pushy at a counter. Say vorrei, per me, or just the item and per favore.
steps.context: Standing at the banco is cheaper than sitting at a table, where there may be table service at a higher price.

answer.it: Vorrei un bicchiere d'acqua, per favore.
answer.en: I'd like a glass of water, please.

ask.en: At the counter or at a table?

mission.goal: Ask politely for a glass of water.

say.it: Vorrei un bicchiere d'acqua, per favore.
say.en: I'd like a glass of water, please.

steps.title: What are you having?
steps.how_to: How to ask what someone is having, and say what you'll have.
steps.intro: You'll be able to ask a friend or a stranger what they're having, say what you'll have, and offer to pay. You'll use it whenever you go to the bar with someone.

examples.it: Prendo anch'io un caffè. Offro io!
examples.en: I'll have a coffee too. It's on me!

steps.notice: Italians "take" food and drink, so use prendo, not "ho". "Ho un caffè" means "I've got a coffee". Use prendi with a friend and prende with someone you address politely.

ask.it: Io prendo un caffè. E tu?
ask.en: I'm having an espresso. And you?

answer.it: Prendo anch'io un caffè. Offro io!
answer.en: I'll have a coffee too. It's on me!

mission.goal: Say what you'll have and offer to pay for a friend.

say.en: I'll have an espresso. It's on me!

steps.title: Numbers up to 2,000
steps.how_to: How to say numbers from twenty to two thousand.
steps.intro: You'll be able to understand and say prices with bigger numbers. You'll need them at every till.
steps.notice: Numbers are built just like in English, but the tens lose their last vowel before uno and otto: ventuno, ventotto, never ventiuno. Ventitré and trentatré take an accent, and two thousand is duemila, not duemille.

mission.goal: Ask the total and listen for the number.

steps.title: Saying prices in euros
steps.how_to: How to say and understand a price in euros and cents.
steps.intro: You'll be able to say a price out loud and follow it when someone tells you. You'd use it at the bar, at the bakery and at the market.
steps.notice: Euro never changes: it's due euro, never 'due euros'. The cents usually go unsaid, so quattro e cinquanta means 4.50. If a price sounds odd, just ask again.

mission.goal: Order, ask the total, and repeat the price you hear.

say.it: Un caffè e un cornetto. Quant'è?
say.en: An espresso and a croissant. How much is that?

steps.title: Asking how much
steps.how_to: How to ask the price of one thing, several things, or the total.
steps.intro: You'll be able to ask what things cost at a stall or a counter. You'd say it before you buy.

examples.it: Un caffè e un cornetto. Quant'è?
examples.en: An espresso and a croissant. How much is that?

steps.notice: One thing takes costa and several things take costano. There's no word for 'it': you just say Quanto costa? For the total of everything, use Quant'è?

ask.en: How do you ask the total?

ask.it: Come chiede il prezzo del pane?
ask.en: How do you ask the price of the bread?

ask.it: Come chiede il prezzo delle pesche?
ask.en: How do you ask the price of the peaches?

mission.goal: Ask the price of several things at a stall.

steps.title: Paying by card or cash
steps.how_to: How to ask to pay by card and say you'll pay cash.
steps.intro: You'll be able to choose how you pay and hand over your money politely. You'd say it at any till.

examples.it: Pago in contanti. Ecco a Lei.
examples.en: I'll pay cash. Here you are.

steps.notice: After posso, the next verb stays in its basic form: posso pagare, never posso pago. Ecco a Lei is polite; with a friend say Ecco a te, or just Ecco.
steps.context: Take the scontrino when it's handed to you.

ask.it: Come dice che paga in contanti?
ask.en: How do you say you'll pay cash?

ask.it: Come chiede di pagare con la carta?
ask.en: How do you ask to pay by card?

ask.it: Come dà i soldi al cassiere?
ask.en: How do you hand the money to the cashier?

mission.goal: Ask to pay by card at the till.

steps.title: When you have no change
steps.how_to: How to answer when the shopkeeper asks if you have change.
steps.intro: You'll be able to understand Ha moneta? and say you haven't got small coins. It happens when you pay with a big note.

examples.en: Sorry, I haven't got any change.

examples.it: Va bene. Ecco il resto: otto euro.
examples.en: That's fine. Here's your change: eight euros.

steps.notice: Ha moneta? and Ha spiccioli? mean the same thing, and you only need to understand them. Your answer is Mi dispiace, non ho spiccioli.
steps.context: Cashiers often ask 'Ha moneta?' to avoid breaking a big note.

ask.it: Come dice 'Here you are, ten euros'?
ask.en: How do you say 'Here you are, ten euros'?

answer.en: Sorry, I haven't got any change.

ask.it: Il giornale costa due euro. Ha spiccioli?
ask.en: The newspaper is two euros. Have you got any coins?

answer.it: Mi dispiace, non ho spiccioli. Ecco dieci euro.
answer.en: Sorry, I haven't got any change. Here's ten euros.

mission.goal: Pay for a newspaper with a ten-euro note and say you have no change.
